title: A Lump That Shatters Under a Hammer Is a Liquid, and It Has Dripped for Over 90 Years
hook: The University of Queensland's pitch funnel was started in 1927, and nine drops had fallen by 2014
summary: Pitch that shatters under a hammer is actually a very slow liquid. Nine drops had fallen by 2014, and two custodians never saw one fall.

text: This experiment has been running at the University of Queensland for over 90 years.
At room temperature it feels hard, and a hammer blow shatters it easily.

panels.text: It shatters, but it's a liquid? That makes no sense.

text: But according to the university, this substance is a liquid even at room temperature.
It's just about 100 billion times thicker than water.
In 1927, Thomas Parnell, the physics department's first professor, poured melted pitch into a funnel.
It took 8 years for the first drop to fall.
According to the university, nine drops have fallen so far, and the last one was in April 2014.
Professor John Mainstone, in the photo, ran this experiment for 52 years starting in 1961.
But he died without ever seeing a drop fall.
The same was true of Professor Parnell, who started it.
